1486500577691, "ts_us": 1486500577691547, "ts_ns": 1486500577691547930 } } This portion of the event is much longer, but like the event’s key, it also has a schema and a payload. The schema contains a Kafka Connect schema named dbserver1.inventory.customers.Envelope (version 1) that can contain five fields: op A required field that contains a string value describing the type of operation. Values for the MySQL connector are c for create (or insert), u for update, d for delete, and r for read (in the case of a snapshot). before An optional field that, if present, contains the state of the row before the event occurred. The structure will be described by the dbserver1.inventory.customers.Value Kafka Connect schema, which the dbserver1 connector uses for all rows in the inventory.customers table. after An optional field that, if present, contains the state of the row after the event occurred. The structure is described by the same dbserver1.inventory.customers.Value Kafka Connect schema used in before. source A required field that contains a structure describing the source metadata for the event, which in the case of MySQL, contains several fields: the connector name, the name of the binlog file where the event was recorded, the position in that binlog file where the event appeared, the row within the event (if there is more than one), the names of the affected database and table, the MySQL thread ID that made the change, whether this event was part of a snapshot, and, if available, the MySQL server ID, and the timestamp in seconds. ts_ms An optional field that, if present, contains the time (using the system clock in the JVM running the Kafka Connect task) at which the connector processed the event. The JSON representations of the events are much longer than the rows they describe. This is because, with every event key and value, Kafka Connect ships the schema that describes the payload. Over time, this structure may change. However, having the schemas for the key and the value in the event itself makes it much easier for consuming applications to understand the messages, especially as they evolve over time. The Debezium MySQL connector constructs these schemas based upon the structure of the database tables. If you use DDL statements to alter the table definitions in the MySQL databases, the connector reads these DDL statements and updates its Kafka Connect schemas. This is the only way that each event is structured exactly like the table from where it originated at the time the event occurred. However, the Kafka topic containing all of the events for a single table might have events that correspond to each state of the table definition. The JSON converter includes the key and value schemas in every message, so it does produce very verbose events. Alternatively, you can use Apache Avro as a serialization format, which results in far smaller event messages. This is because it transforms each Kafka Connect schema into an Avro schema and stores the Avro schemas in a separate Schema Registry service. Thus, when the Avro converter serializes an event message, it places only a unique identifier for the schema along with an Avro-encoded binary representation of the value. As a result, the serialized messages that are transferred over the wire and stored in Kafka are far smaller than what you have seen here. In fact, the Avro Converter is able to use Avro schema evolution techniques to maintain the history of each schema in the Schema Registry. Compare the event’s key and value schemas to the state of the inventory database. In the terminal that is running the MySQL command line client, run the following statement: mysql> SELECT * FROM customers; +------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+ | id | first_name | last_name | email | +------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+ | 1001 | Sally | Thomas | [email protected] | | 1002 | George | Bailey | [email protected] | | 1003 | Edward | Walker | [email protected] | | 1004 | Anne | Kretchmar | [email protected] | +------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+ 4 rows in set (0.00 sec) This shows that the event records you reviewed match the records in the database. Updating the database and viewing the update event By updating a record in the database and observing the change event that the Debezium MySQL connector captures, you can learn how to identify what changed in a commit and compare events to determine their sequence. Procedure In the terminal that is running the MySQL command line client, run the following statement: mysql> UPDATE customers SET first_name='Anne Marie' WHERE id=1004; Query OK, 1 row affected (0.05 sec) Rows matched: 1 Changed: 1 Warnings: 0 View the updated customers table: mysql> SELECT * FROM customers; +------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+ | id | first_name | last_name | email | +------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+ | 1001 | Sally | Thomas | [email protected] | | 1002 | George | Bailey | [email protected] | | 1003 | Edward | Walker | [email protected] | | 1004 | Anne Marie | Kretchmar | [email protected] | +------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+ 4 rows in set (0.00 sec) Switch to the terminal running watch-topic to see a new fifth event. By changing a record in the customers table, the Debezium MySQL connector generated a new event. You should see two new JSON documents: one for the event’s key, and one for the new event’s value. Here are the details of the key for the update event (formatted for readability): { "schema": { "type": "struct", "name": "dbserver1.inventory.customers.Key", "optional": false, "fields": [ { "field": "id", "type": "int32", "optional": false } ] }, "payload": { "id": 1004 } } This key is the same as the key for the previous events. Here is that new event’s value. There are no changes in the schema section, so only the payload section is shown (formatted for readability): { "schema": {...}, "payload": { "before": { "id": 1004, "first_name": "Anne", "last_name": "Kretchmar", "email": "[email protected]" }, "after": { "id": 1004, "first_name": "Anne Marie", "last_name": "Kretchmar", "email": "[email protected]" }, "source": { "name": "3.7.0.Beta1", "name": "dbserver1", "server_id": 223344, "ts_sec": 1486501486, "gtid": null, "file": "mysql-bin.000003", "pos": 364, "row": 0, "snapshot": null, "thread": 3, "db": "inventory", "table": "customers" }, "op": "u", "ts_ms": 1486501486308, "ts_us": 1486501486308910, "ts_ns": 1486501486308910814 } } The following list describes select fields in the preceding example of the payload of an update event value: before The before field shows the values that were present in the row before the update. The original first_name value is Anne. after The after field shows the state of the row after the update event. The first_name value is now Anne Marie. source The source field structure has many of the same values as before, except that the ts_sec and pos fields have changed. In some circumstances, the file value might also change. op Shows the type of operation that the event describes. The u value indicates that change was due to an update event. ts_ms, ts_us, ts_ns Displays timestamps in milliseconds, microseconds, and nanoseconds that indicate when the connector processed the event. The time is based on the system clock in the JVM that runs the Kafka Connect task. By viewing the payload section, you can learn several important things about the update event: By comparing the before and after structures, you can determine what actually changed in the affected row because of the commit. By reviewing the source structure, you can find information about MySQL’s record of the change (providing traceability). By comparing the payload section of an event to other events in the same topic (or a different topic), you can determine whether the event occurred before, after, or as part of the same MySQL commit as another event. Deleting a record in the database and viewing the delete event By deleting a record in the database and observing the change event that the Debezium MySQL connector captures, you can learn how Debezium represents deletions and how Kafka log compaction handles tombstone events. Procedure In the terminal that is running the MySQL command line client, run the following statement: mysql> DELETE FROM customers WHERE id=1004; Query OK, 1 row affected (0.00 sec) If the above command fails with a foreign key constraint violation, then you must remove the reference of the customer address from the addresses table using the following statement: mysql> DELETE FROM addresses WHERE customer_id=1004; Switch to the terminal running watch-topic to see two new events. By deleting a row in the customers table, the Debezium MySQL connector generated two new events. Review the key and value for the first new event. Here are the details of the key for the first new event (formatted for readability): { "schema": { "type": "struct", "name": "dbserver1.inventory.customers.Key", "optional": false, "fields": [ { "field": "id", "type": "int32", "optional": false } ] }, "payload": { "id": 1004 } } This key is the same as the key in the previous two events you looked at. Here is the value of the first new event (formatted for readability): { "schema": {...}, "payload": { "before": { "id": 1004, "first_name": "Anne Marie", "last_name": "Kretchmar", "email": "[email protected]" }, "after": null, "source": { "name": "3.7.0.Beta1", "name": "dbserver1", "server_id": 223344, "ts_sec": 1486501558, "gtid": null, "file": "mysql-bin.000003", "pos": 725, "row": 0, "snapshot": null, "thread": 3, "db": "inventory", "table": "customers" }, "op": "d", "ts_ms": 1486501558315, "ts_us": 1486501558315901, "ts_ns": 1486501558315901687 } } The following list describes select fields in the preceding example of a delete event value: before The before field shows the state of the row before its deletion. after Shows the state of the field after the deletion. The value of the after field is null, because the row no longer exists. source The source field structure has many of the same values as before, the deletion occurred, except that the values of the ts_sec and pos fields have changed. In some circumstances, the file value might also change. op Shows the type of operation that the event describes. The op field value is d, indicating that the record was deleted. ts_ms, ts_us, ts_ns Displays timestamps in milliseconds, microseconds, and nanoseconds that indicate when the connector processed the event. The time is based on the system clock in the JVM that runs the Kafka Connect task. Thus, this event provides a consumer with the information that it needs to process the removal of the row. The event record also provides the old values, because some consumers might require them to properly handle the removal. Review the key and value for the second new event. Here is the key for the second new event (formatted for readability): { "schema": { "type": "struct", "name": "dbserver1.inventory.customers.Key" "optional": false, "fields": [ { "field": "id", "type": "int32", "optional": false } ] }, "payload": { "id": 1004 } } Once again, this key is exactly the same key as in the previous three events you looked at. Here is the value of that same event (formatted for readability): { "schema": null, "payload": null } If Kafka is set up to be log compacted, it will remove older messages from the topic if there is at least one message later in the topic with same key. This last event is called a tombstone event, because it has a key and an empty value. This means that Kafka will remove all prior messages with the same key. Even though the prior messages will be removed, the tombstone event means that consumers can still read the topic from the beginning and not miss any events. Restarting the Kafka Connect service When the Kafka Connect service goes offline and restarts, Debezium resumes capturing database changes from the point where it stopped, without missing any events. The Kafka Connect service automatically manages tasks for its registered connectors. Therefore, if it goes offline, when it restarts, it will start any non-running tasks. This means that even if Debezium is not running, it can still report changes in a database. Procedure Open a new terminal and use it to stop the connect container that is running the Kafka Connect service: $ docker stop connect The connect container is stopped, and the Kafka Connect service gracefully shuts down. Because you ran the container with the --rm option, Docker removes the container once it stops. While the service is down, switch to the terminal for the MySQL command line client, and add a few records: mysql> INSERT INTO customers VALUES (default, "Sarah", "Thompson", "[email protected]"); mysql> INSERT INTO customers VALUES (default, "Kenneth", "Anderson", "[email protected]"); The records are added to the database. However, because Kafka Connect is not running, watch-topic does not record any updates. In a production system, you would have enough brokers to handle the producers and consumers, and to maintain a minimum number of in-sync replicas for each topic. Therefore, if enough brokers failed such that there were no longer the minimum number of ISRs, Kafka would become unavailable. In this scenario, producers (like the Debezium connectors) and consumers will wait for the Kafka cluster or network to recover. This means that, temporarily, your consumers might not see any change events as data is changed in the databases. This is because no change events are being produced. As soon as the Kafka cluster is restarted or the network recovers, Debezium will resume producing change events, and your consumers will resume consuming events where they left off. Open a new terminal, and use it to restart the Kafka Connect service in a container. This command starts Kafka Connect using the same options you used when you initially started it: $ docker run -it --rm --name connect -p 8083:8083 -e GROUP_ID=1 -e BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS=kafka:9092 -e CONFIG_STORAGE_TOPIC=my_connect_configs -e OFFSET_STORAGE_TOPIC=my_connect_offsets -e STATUS_STORAGE_TOPIC=my_connect_statuses --link kafka:kafka --link mysql:mysql quay.io/debezium/connect:3.7 The Kafka Connect service starts, connects to Kafka, reads the previous service’s configuration, and starts the registered connectors that will resume where they last left off. These events are create events that are similar to what you saw previously. As you see, Debezium still reports all of the changes in a database even when it is not running (as long as it is restarted before the MySQL database purges from its binlog the commits that were missed). Cleaning up After you are finished with the tutorial, you can use Docker to stop all of the running containers. Procedure Stop each of the containers: $ docker stop mysqlterm watcher connect mysql kafka Docker stops each container. Because you used the --rm option when you started them, Docker also removes them. If you use Podman, run the following command: $ podman pod kill dbz $ podman pod rm dbz Verify that all of the processes have stopped and have been removed: $ docker ps -a If any of the processes are still running, stop them using docker stop <process-name> or docker stop <containerId>. Next steps After completing the tutorial, consider the following next steps: Explore the tutorial further. Use the MySQL command line client to add, modify, and remove rows in the database tables, and see the effect on the topics. You may need to run a separate watch-topic command for each topic. Keep in mind that you cannot remove a row that is referenced by a foreign key. Try running the tutorial with Debezium connectors for Postgres, MongoDB, SQL Server, and Oracle. You can use the Docker Compose version of this tutorial located in the Debezium examples repository. Docker Compose files are provided for running the tutorial with MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB, SQL Server, and Oracle.

Please let us know if you encounter any problems while using this feature. Also please reach out if you have requirements for specific sinks to be supported by HyperCDC Server or even would be interested in contributing the required implementation.

HyperCDC provides a ready-to-use application that streams change events from a source database to messaging infrastructure like Amazon Kinesis, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Apache Pulsar, Redis (Stream), or NATS JetStream. For streaming change events to Apache Kafka, it is recommended to deploy the HyperCDC connectors via Kafka Connect.

Installation

To install the server download and unpack the server distribution archive:

  • HyperCDC Server distribution

The above links refers to the nightly snapshot build of the HyperCDC main branch. If you are looking for a non-snapshot version, please select the appropriate version of this documentation in the menu to the right.

A directory named hypercdc-server will be created with these contents:

hypercdc-server/
|-- CHANGELOG.md
|-- config
|-- CONTRIBUTING.md
|-- COPYRIGHT.txt
|-- hypercdc-server-3.7.0.Beta1-runner.jar
|-- lib
|-- LICENSE-3rd-PARTIES.txt
|-- LICENSE.txt
|-- README.md
`-- run.sh

The server is started using run.sh script, dependencies are stored in the lib directory, and the directory config contains configuration files.

In case of using the Oracle connector you will have to add to the lib directory the ORACLE JDBC driver (if using XStream also the XStream API files), explained here: Obtaining the Oracle JDBC driver and XStream API files

Configuration

HyperCDC Server uses MicroProfile Configuration for configuration. This means that the application can be configured from disparate sources like configuration files, environment variables, system properties etc.

Configuration properties that contain the $ character are normally interpreted by Quarkus for property expansion. If a property value includes a $ character as a prefix, such as ${my.property}, the Microprofile configuration parser determines that the value is a property expression and attempts to expand it.

To prevent the parser from attempting to expand values that use this syntax, escape the $ prefix with a second $ character; that is, provide the value as $${my.property}. The value of the property is then passed to HyperCDC as ${my.property}.

The main configuration file is config/application.properties. There are multiple sections configured:

  • hypercdc.source is for source connector configuration; each instance of HyperCDC Server runs exactly one connector

  • hypercdc.sink is for the sink system configuration

  • hypercdc.format is for the output serialization format configuration

  • hypercdc.transforms is for the configuration of message transformations

  • hypercdc.predicates is for the configuration of message transformation predicates

An example configuration file can look like so:

hypercdc.sink.type=kinesis
hypercdc.sink.kinesis.region=eu-central-1
hypercdc.source.connector.class=io.hypercdc.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector
hypercdc.source.offset.storage.file.filename=data/offsets.dat
hypercdc.source.offset.flush.interval.ms=0
hypercdc.source.database.hostname=localhost
hypercdc.source.database.port=5432
hypercdc.source.database.user=postgres
hypercdc.source.database.password=postgres
hypercdc.source.database.dbname=postgres
hypercdc.source.topic.prefix=tutorial
hypercdc.source.schema.include.list=inventory

In this configuration file example:

  • The sink is setup for AWS Kinesis in region eu-central-1

  • The source connector is setup for PostgreSQL using the default HyperCDC decoderbufs plugin. If using PostgreSQL’s built-in pgoutput plugin, set hypercdc.source.plugin.name=pgoutput

  • The source connector is set to capture events from a schema named inventory. If you want to capture all changes in the database, remove this line. Otherwise, update this line to correspond to your preferred schema or tables.

  • The source offset will be stored in a file named offsets.dat in the data directory. Note that you might need to create this directory to prevent an error on startup.

Source configuration

The source configuration uses the same configuration properties that are described on the specific connector documentation pages (just with hypercdc.source prefix), together with few more specific ones, necessary for running outside of Kafka Connect:

Property Default Description

hypercdc.source.connector.class

The name of the Java class implementing the source connector.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage

org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.FileOffsetBackingStore

Class to use for storing and retrieving offsets for non-Kafka deployments. Available options

  • org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.FileOffsetBackingStore for non-Kafka deployments

  • org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.MemoryOffsetBackingStore volatile store for test environments

  • io.hypercdc.storage.jdbc.offset.JdbcOffsetBackingStore for database using JDBC

  • io.hypercdc.storage.redis.offset.RedisOffsetBackingStore for Redis deployments

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.file.filename

If using a file offset store (default), the file in which connector offsets are stored for non-Kafka deployments.

hypercdc.source.offset.flush.interval.ms

Defines how frequently the offsets are flushed into the file.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.address

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets, an address, formatted as host:port, at which the Redis target streams are provided. If not supplied, will attempt to read hypercdc.sink.redis.address

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.user

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets, a user name used to communicate with Redis. If the redis.address configuration is not supplied, and the redis.address is taken from the Redis sink, will attempt to load the value from hypercdc.sink.redis.user

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.password

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets, a password (of respective user) used to communicate with Redis. A password must be set if a user is set. If the redis.address configuration is not supplied, and the redis.address is taken from the Redis sink, will attempt to load the value from hypercdc.sink.redis.password

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.ssl.enabled

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets, whether or not to use SSL to communicate with Redis. If the redis.address configuration is not supplied, and the redis.address is taken from the Redis sink, will attempt to load the value from hypercdc.sink.redis.ssl.enabled. Default is 'false'

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.ssl.hostname.verification.enabled

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets, whether or not to enable hostname verification with Redis. If the redis.address configuration is not supplied, and the redis.address is taken from the Redis sink, will attempt to load the value from hypercdc.sink.redis.ssl.hostname.verification.enabled. Default is 'false'

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.ssl.truststore.path

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets with SSL enabled, the path to the trust store file. If set, Redis connections will use this property over other configuration or system properties.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.ssl.truststore.password

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets with SSL enabled, the password for the trust store file. If set, Redis connections will use this property over other configuration or system properties.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.ssl.truststore.type

JKS

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets with SSL enabled, the type of the trust store file. If set, Redis connections will use this property over other configuration or system properties.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.ssl.keystore.path

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets with SSL enabled, the path to the key store file. If set, Redis connections will use this property over other configuration or system properties.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.ssl.keystore.password

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets with SSL enabled, the password for the key store file. If set, Redis connections will use this property over other configuration or system properties.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.ssl.keystore.type

JKS

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets with SSL enabled, the type of the key store file. If set, Redis connections will use this property over other configuration or system properties.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.key

(Optional) If using Redis to store offsets, define the hash key in redis. If the redis.key configuration is not supplied, and the default value is metadata:hypercdc:offsets

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.wait.enabled

false

If using Redis to store offsets, enables wait for replica. In case Redis is configured with a replica shard, this allows to verify that the data has been written to the replica. For more information see Redis WAIT command.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.wait.timeout.ms

1000

If using Redis to store offsets, defines the timeout in milliseconds when waiting for replica. Must have a positive value.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.wait.retry.enabled

false

If using Redis to store offsets, enables retry on wait for replica failure.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.wait.retry.delay.ms

1000

If using Redis to store offsets, defines the delay of retry on wait for replica failure.

hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.cluster.enabled

false

If you configure HyperCDC Server to store offsets in Redis, set this property to specify whether to use Redis Cluster mode. Set the value to true to configure HyperCDC to use a JedisCluster client to route offset data to Redis nodes.

hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal

io.hypercdc.storage.kafka.history.KafkaSchemaHistory

Some of the connectors (e.g MySQL, SQL Server, Db2, Oracle) track the database schema evolution over time and stores this data in a database schema history. This is by default based on Kafka. There are also other options available

  • io.hypercdc.storage.file.history.FileSchemaHistory for non-Kafka deployments

  • io.hypercdc.relational.history.MemorySchemaHistory volatile store for test environments

  • io.hypercdc.storage.redis.history.RedisSchemaHistory for Redis deployments

  • io.hypercdc.storage.rocketmq.history.RocketMqSchemaHistory for RocketMQ deployments

  • io.hypercdc.storage.azure.blob.history.AzureBlobSchemaHistory for Azure Blob Storage deployments

hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.file.filename

The name and location of the file to which FileSchemaHistory persists its data.

hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.address

The Redis host:port to connect to if using RedisSchemaHistory.

hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.user

The Redis user to use if using RedisSchemaHistory.

hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.password

The Redis password to use if using RedisSchemaHistory.

hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.ssl.enabled

Use SSL connection if using RedisSchemaHistory.

Before the messages are delivered to the sink, they can run through a sequence of transformations. The server supports single message transformations defined by Kafka Connect. Asynchronous Engine Properties

By default, HyperCDC server uses the asynchronous embedded engine (AsyncEmbeddedEngine) as its processing engine. You can configure the following options for the asynchronous embedded engine:

Property

Default

Description

record.processing.threads

Threads allocated on demand, based on the workload and the number of available CPU cores.

The number of threads that are available to process change event records. If no value is specified (the default), the engine uses the Java ThreadPoolExecutor to dynamically adjust the number of threads, based on the current workload. Maximum number of threads is number of CPU cores on given machine. If a value is specified, the engine uses the Java fixed thread pool method to create a thread pool with the specified number of threads. To use all available cores on given machine, set the placeholder value, AVAILABLE_CORES.

record.processing.shutdown.timeout.ms

1000

Maximum time, in milliseconds, that the engine allows for processing pending records after a task shutdown is called.

task.management.timeout.ms

180,000 (3 min)

Time, in milliseconds, that the engine waits for a task’s lifecycle management operations (starting and stopping) to complete.

Enabling message filtering

HyperCDC Server provides filter SMTs (Single Message Transformations) capability. See Message Filtering for more details. However, for security reasons it’s not enabled by default and has to be explicitly enabled when HyperCDC Server is started. To enable it, set environment variable ENABLE_HYPERCDC_SCRIPTING to true. This will add hypercdc-scripting jar file and JSR 223 implementations (currently Groovy and graalvm.js) jar files into the server class path. These jar files are contained in opt_lib directory of the HyperCDC Server distribution.

hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.dynamicpartitionrouting

An optional setting that controls the behavior of dynamic partition routing. There are three possible values:

  • default: If the record key is not null, it is used as the batch partition key. Else, if the record’s partition ID is not null, events are batched and routed to the specified partition ID. Otherwise, round-robin routing is applied. This is the default when no value is provided.

  • key: If the record key is not null, it is used as the batch partition key. Otherwise, round-robin routing is applied.

  • partitionid: If the record’s partition ID is not null, events are batched and routed to the specified partition ID. Otherwise, round-robin routing is applied.

The hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.dynamicpartitionrouting configuration is only applied when both of the following options are unset:

  • hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.partitionkey

(Optional) The identifier of the Event Hub partition that the events will be sent to. Use this if you want all the change events received by HyperCDC to be sent to a specific partition in Event Hubs. Do not use if you have specified hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.partitionkey

hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.partitionkey

(Optional) The partition key will be used to hash the events. Use this if you want all the change events received by HyperCDC to be sent to a specific partition in Event Hubs. Do not use if you have specified hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.partitionid

No default value

(Optional) Specifies the hash function that HyperCDC uses to encrypt encrypt Azure Event Hubs message keys.

Specify one of the following values:

  • java

  • md5

  • sha1

  • sha256
Using partitions in EventHubs

By default, when neither of the optional hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.partitionid or hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.partitionkey properties are defined, the EventHubs sink will send events round-robin to all available partitions.

You can enforce all messages to be sent to a single, fixed, partition by setting the hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.partitionid property. Alternatively, you can use the hypercdc.sink.eventhubs.partitionkey property to specify a fixed partition key that EventHubs will use to route all events to a specific partition.

If you have more specific routing requirements you can use the Partition Routing transformer. Ensure that the number of partitions specified in the transformer’s partition.topic.num setting is equal or less to the number of partitions available in your EventHubs namespace, so that events cannot be routed to non-existing partition IDs. As an example, to route all events to 5 partitions based on their source schema name, you can set the following in your application.properties:

# Uses a hash of `source.db` to calculate which partition to send the event to. Ensures all events from the same source schema are sent to the same partition.
hypercdc.transforms=PartitionRouter
hypercdc.transforms.PartitionRouter.type=io.hypercdc.transforms.partitions.PartitionRouting
hypercdc.transforms.PartitionRouter.partition.payload.fields=source.db
hypercdc.transforms.PartitionRouter.partition.topic.num=5

Redis (Stream)

Redis is an open source (BSD licensed) in-memory data structure store, used as a database, cache and message broker. The Stream is a data type which models a log data structure in a more abstract way. It implements powerful operations to overcome the limitations of a log file.

HyperCDC can use either a single Redis instance or use Redis Cluster mode for sink operations:

Single instance mode

Connects to a single Redis server instance.

Cluster mode

Connects to a Redis Cluster for high availability and horizontal scaling.

To enable Redis Cluster mode, set the hypercdc.sink.redis.cluster.enabled property to true and provide comma-separated host:port addresses in the hypercdc.sink.redis.address property.

Redis Configuration Examples

The following examples show complete application.properties configurations for connecting HyperCDC Server to a Redis sink in both single-instance and cluster deployment modes.

Single Instance Mode

Use the following configuration when connecting to a single Redis instance for sink, offset storage, and schema history.

# Sink configuration
hypercdc.sink.type=redis
hypercdc.sink.redis.address=localhost:6379
hypercdc.sink.redis.password=password
hypercdc.sink.redis.cluster.enabled=false

# Offset storage configuration
hypercdc.source.offset.storage=io.hypercdc.storage.redis.offset.RedisOffsetBackingStore
hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.address=localhost:6379
hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.password=password
hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.cluster.enabled=false

# Schema history storage configuration
hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal=io.hypercdc.storage.redis.history.RedisSchemaHistory
hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.address=localhost:6379
hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.password=password
hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.cluster.enabled=false
Cluster Mode

Use the following configuration when connecting HyperCDC Server to a Redis Cluster, specifying multiple node addresses for sink, offset storage, and schema history.

# Sink configuration
hypercdc.sink.type=redis
hypercdc.sink.redis.address=redis-node-1:7001,redis-node-2:7002,redis-node-3:7003
hypercdc.sink.redis.password=password
hypercdc.sink.redis.cluster.enabled=true

# Offset storage configuration
hypercdc.source.offset.storage=io.hypercdc.storage.redis.offset.RedisOffsetBackingStore
hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.address=redis-node-1:7001,redis-node-2:7002,redis-node-3:7003
hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.password=password
hypercdc.source.offset.storage.redis.cluster.enabled=true

# Schema history storage configuration
hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal=io.hypercdc.storage.redis.history.RedisSchemaHistory
hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.address=redis-node-1:7001,redis-node-2:7002,redis-node-3:7003
hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.password=password
hypercdc.source.schema.history.internal.redis.cluster.enabled=true
If you configure HyperCDC to use Redis Cluster mode, ensure that your Redis Cluster is properly configured and accessible. The HyperCDC Server instance must be able to communicate with the cluster nodes.

NATS JetStream

NATS has a built-in distributed persistence system called JetStream which enables new functionalities and higher qualities of service on top of the base 'Core NATS' functionalities and qualities of service.

Property Default Description

hypercdc.sink.type

Must be set to nats-jetstream.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.stream-name

HyperCDCStream

Optional custom name for the stream that HyperCDC creates.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.url

URL (or comma separated list of URLs) to a node or nodes in the cluster formatted as nats://host:port.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.create-stream

If true, a basic stream will be created.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.subjects

*.*.*

A comma separated list of JetStream subjects, or messaging channel names. You can specify entries that contain wildcards, such as test.inventory.*

To capture both schema change events and data change events, you must specify both the topic prefix and a wildcard pattern. For example, if your hypercdc.source.topic.prefix is myapp, configure subjects as myapp,myapp.> or myapp,myapp..

Data change events are published to table-specific subjects (for example, myapp.database.table) The value myapp.> matches any number of subject levels; similarly myapp.. matches exactly two levels after the prefix.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.storage

memory

Controls how the messages are saved in the stream. Can be memory or file.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.auth.jwt

No default value

Specifies the identity of the NATS server client. Add this property to the configuration to enable JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication with NATS. To use JWT authentication with NATS, you must specify the NKey seed. Do not enable JWT authentication, if password authentication is enabled.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.auth.seed

No default value

When JWT authentication is enabled for NATS, use this property so specify the NKey seed that represents the HyperCDC user. HyperCDC uses the specified NKey seed to derive a private key. It then uses the private key to cryptographically sign the nonce challenge that the NATS server issues during the authentication process. HyperCDC returns the signed nonce to the server, along with the public key for the specified hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.auth.jwt client.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.auth.user

No default value

Specifies the username of the authorized NAT user. When this property is present in the configuration, password authentication with NATS is enabled. To use password authentication with NATS, specify a hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.auth.password. Do not enable password authentication if JWT authentication is enabled.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.auth.password

No default value

Specifies the password to use when password authentication is enabled.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.async.enabled

true

(Optional) A Boolean value that specifies whether HyperCDC can stream asynchronously to a NATS JetStream server.

hypercdc.sink.nats-jetstream.async.timeout.ms

5000

(Optional) Specifies the maximum time, in milliseconds, that HyperCDC waits for acknowledgment from the NATS server after it sends a batch of messages for asynchronous processing. During asynchronous processing, each message is published with a timeout specified by asyncTimeoutMs.

If you need a more configurable stream, it can be created with nats cli. More about streams at: https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream/streams

Apache Fluss

Apache Fluss is a streaming storage built for real-time analytics, providing unified streaming and batch processing capabilities with high performance, low latency, and strong consistency guarantees. HyperCDC Server can publish change events to Apache Fluss, supporting both primary key tables for upsert/delete operations and log tables for append-only streaming.

Apache Fluss requires connectors to be configured with schemas enabled. Schemaless change events are not supported.

auto

Determines the write mode selection based on primary key presence. Valid values:

auto

Automatically selects between append and upsert mode based on whether the table has a primary key.

upsert

Requires tables to have a primary key and performs insert/update/delete operations.

Pravega

Pravega is a cloud-native storage system for event streams and data streams. This sink offers two modes: non-transactional and transactional. The non-transactional mode individually writes each event in a HyperCDC batch to Pravega. The transactional mode writes the HyperCDC batch to a Pravega transaction that commits when the batch is completed.

The Pravega sink expects destination scope and streams to already be created.

Qdrant Sink

Qdrant is an open-source vector database optimized for vector similarity search and extended with powerful filtering capabilities. It’s designed for high-load applications, and it enables you to efficiently store, manage, and search embedding vectors. You can use Qdrant to process vector datatypes that are captured directly from a source database, or you can use a transformation to calculate embeddings from message fields, and then send those embeddings to the database for processing.

Qdrant sink ingests incoming messages and upserts the after part of each message into a collection. When a delete message arrives, the matching record is removed from the collection.

The sink behaves according to the following rules:

  • Each HyperCDC collection or table is mapped to a Qdrant collection.

  • Primary keys are required and are used as Qdrant point IDs (only INT64 and UUID are supported).

  • FloatVector and DoubleVector data can serve as sources for Qdrant vectors.

  • Non-primary key and non-vector fields are mapped to Qdrant payloads.

InstructLab

InstructLab is a community-driven project for augmenting large language models (LLMs) for use in generative artificial intelligence applications. Working with InstructLab, users who identify gaps in the capabilities of a base model can collaboratively develop a taxonomy to augment the model, with each contributor providing specific expertise and skills.

HyperCDC Server enables you to automate the process of adding skills and knowledge into a taxonomy by configuring a data sink based on InstructLab question and answer (qna.yml) files. The sink configuration defines a series of mappings that are used to derive question, answer, and context values from an event stream. These mappings can source values directly from fields within the event payload, headers, or statically configured constants. Periodically, users can then use InstructLab to train the model to take advantage of the new skills and knowledge added to the taxonomies.

A comma-separated list of the symbolic names of taxonomy mappings.

Specifies a Mapping definition to use as the seed example’s question attribute in the qna.yml file. This is required.

Specifies the taxonomy domain, a series of directories separated by / to the qna.yml, excluding the taxonomy base path. For example, a value of a/b and a base path of /taxonomy represents /taxonomy/a/b/qna.yml.
Mapping definition

In the InstructLab sink configuration, you can set properties to specify how HyperCDC Server maps fields in event messages to question, answer, and contextattributes in an InstructLab qna.yml file.

For each attribute type that you want to populate in the qna.yml file, you specify a mapping prefix that determines the message field from which HyperCDC extracts the value. You can specify the following prefix values:

Value

If you prefix a mapping definition with the string value:, HyperCDC extracts the value of the specified field from the incoming event payload. For example, to populate an InstructLab question attribute with the value of the abc field in the event payload, set the hypercdc.sink.instructlab.taxonomy.<name>.question property to value:abc. When HyperCDC processes the message it takes the value of the payload field abc and adds it as a question attribute in the qna.yml file.

For events that have a HyperCDC-structured payload, HyperCDC extracts the specified field from the after section of the payload. If the event is flattened, the field is sourced directly from the event’s value.

Header

If you prefix a mapping definition with the string header:, HyperCDC extracts the value of the specified header field of the incoming event message. For example, if you specify the mapping header:h1, when HyperCDC detects a header with the name h1 in a source message, it extracts the value of the h1 field.

Constant

If the mapping definition does not include the header: or value: prefixes, when HyperCDC detects instances of the specified value in incoming messages, it treats them as constants, and uses them as-is. Use this option when you want to map the value of a specific static constant to an attribute in the qna.yml file.

The JDBC sink writes change events directly to a relational database using JDBC. It uses the HyperCDC JDBC connector to support a wide variety of database dialects, including CockroachDB, Db2, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SingleStore, SQL Server, and StarRocks.

The sink supports idempotent writes by using upsert semantics, basic schema evolution to automatically create or alter destination tables, and delete propagation.

The JDBC sink requires the appropriate JDBC driver for the target database to be available on the classpath. The HyperCDC Server distribution does not include any JDBC drivers for target databases, so you must add the driver for your destination database manually to the lib/ directory.

Although the JDBC sink reuses the HyperCDC JDBC sink connector, HyperCDC Server does not currently provide the same delivery guarantees that are available when running the connector in other runtimes such as Kafka Connect. In particular, features that depend on the runtime for offset management, exactly-once semantics, or automatic error handling and retries may behave differently or may not be available.

Apache Iceberg

The HyperCDC Apache Iceberg connector is a sink that runs in HyperCDC Server. It consumes database change events from a source HyperCDC connector and writes them to Apache Iceberg tables. This allows for direct replication of a Database (Change Data Capture events) to Iceberg tables on cloud storage or HDFS, eliminating the need for intermediate systems like ETL Tool, Spark or other streaming platforms.

The HyperCDC Iceberg connector supports both upsert and append modes for data replication. When event and key schema information is enabled, the destination Iceberg tables are automatically created upon the initial startup.

The connector provides the following features:

  • Upsert and Append modes.

  • Optimizing batch size.

  • Customizable table naming.

  • Offset and Schema History storage in Iceberg.

  • Automatic schema evolution.

  • It is recommended to use ExtractNewRecordState transformation (event flattening). Key features like upsert mode and automatic primary key detection depend on the flattened event structure produced by this SMT. Without it, the connector can only operate in a more limited append-only mode.

  • The HyperCDC Server sink for Apache Iceberg is a community-maintained, open-source project. Please note that it is maintained in a separate repository, which you can find here: HyperCDC Server Iceberg GitHub

Databricks Zerobus Ingest

The HyperCDC Databricks Zerobus Ingest is a serverless, push-based ingestion service that writes change event records directly into Unity Catalog Delta tables. The service does not require an intermediate message broker. The sink uses OAuth to authenticate with a Databricks service principal and streams each event record to the Delta table that corresponds to the event destination.

The sink uses one of the following routes to deliver event records, as specified by the hypercdc.sink.type property:

zerobus

(recommended) Uses the Databricks Zerobus Java SDK over gRPC.

zerobus-rest

Uses the Zerobus REST API. This method accepts only one HTTP request per record. Select this option for environments that lack a persistent connection.

kafka

Reuses the built-in Kafka sink against the Zerobus Kafka-compatible endpoint. For more information, see Kafka route.

Because Zerobus accepts only JSON objects that match the target table schema, configure HyperCDC to emit flat JSON by applying the ExtractNewRecordState SMT with schemas.enable=false. Delivery uses an at-least-once guarantee. As a result, the sink might deliver the same record more than once. Configure downstream consumers to deduplicate records, for example, by using the source LSN that the record carries. To enable the service to write data to the target table, the following requirements apply:

  • The target table must be a Unity Catalog-managed Delta table.

  • The table must be in the same Databricks region as the workspace.

  • Change Data Feed and column mapping must be disabled.

  • The service principal must have the following permissions:

    • USE CATALOG

    • USE SCHEMA

    • SELECT

    • MODIFY

Specifies the delay, in milliseconds, between stream recovery attempts.

The SDK default.

The SDK default.

In the preceding table, several Zerobus sink properties list the default value The SDK default. The SDK default is the value defined by the version of the Zerobus SDK that is used by the current HyperCDC Server instance.

The SDK default applies only when the property is not specified in the HyperCDC Server configuration. If the property is omitted, the sink uses the SDK-defined value, including any changes introduced by later SDK upgrades. If you specify a value for the property, the configured value takes precedence.

Envelope row contract

Set hypercdc.sink.zerobus.payload.mode to envelope to preserve the change event for downstream materialization instead of mapping it directly onto the target table columns. The max.record.bytes, json.flexible.fields.encoding, idempotency.mode, tombstone.handling.mode, and filter.* properties apply only to this payload mode.

JSON and Protobuf envelope records expose the same logical fields:

Field Description

target_table

The fully qualified Unity Catalog table to which the sink routes the record.

destination

The original HyperCDC destination before the sink resolves the target table.

partition

The event partition, when one is present.

operation

One of create, read, update, delete, truncate, message, change, or tombstone. The sink uses change when the source value does not contain a recognized HyperCDC operation.

idempotency_key

A deterministic sha256:<64 hexadecimal characters> event identity when idempotency.mode is source. Use this field to deduplicate records after an at-least-once replay.

key

The original serialized record key.

value

The original serialized HyperCDC change-event value. The value is null for a tombstone.

source_position

A map containing source partition and offset entries. Entry names use the partition. and offset. prefixes.

headers

The record headers, ordered by header name.

For JSON records, json.flexible.fields.encoding controls whether key, value, source_position, and headers are canonical JSON strings or nested JSON values. For Protobuf records, the sink supplies the descriptor to Zerobus and encodes these flexible fields as canonical JSON strings.

The sink applies configured include filters in the following order: destination, operation, header, and value. Every configured regular expression must match the complete selected value. An event that does not match is skipped and is considered processed when the rest of the batch succeeds. If filter.operations is configured, a tombstone is ingested only when the allowlist includes tombstone, even if tombstone.handling.mode is event.

The sink provides an at-least-once delivery guarantee. For each contiguous target-table group, the sink serializes and validates every record before ingestion, ingests the group, and waits for Zerobus to acknowledge the final record. The sink commits source offsets only after every target-table group in the batch succeeds. If a later group fails, an earlier acknowledged group can be replayed because the source batch remains uncommitted. Use idempotency_key to deduplicate such replays downstream.

The following example configures the JSON envelope contract, deterministic identities, explicit tombstones, and an operation allowlist:

hypercdc.sink.type=zerobus
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.endpoint=<workspace-id>.zerobus.<region>.cloud.databricks.com
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.workspace.url=https://<workspace-host>
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.client.id=<client-id>
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.client.secret=<client-secret>

hypercdc.sink.zerobus.payload.mode=envelope
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.record.format=json
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.max.record.bytes=10000000
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.json.flexible.fields.encoding=string
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.idempotency.mode=source
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.tombstone.handling.mode=event
hypercdc.sink.zerobus.filter.operations=c,r,u,d,t,m,tombstone

Kafka route

As an alternative to the zerobus and zerobus-rest routes, you can reuse the built-in kafka sink to write to the Zerobus Kafka-compatible endpoint. This route uses the standard Kafka producer with SASL_SSL and the OAUTHBEARER mechanism. Authentication is handled by io.hypercdc.server.databricks.zerobus.ZerobusOAuthBearerLoginCallbackHandler, which performs the OAuth token exchange and attaches the Unity Catalog authorization details that Zerobus requires.

Because this route uses the generic kafka sink rather than the Zerobus sink, the data type normalization that the Data type mapping section describes does not apply. Instead, the emitted JSON must match the target Delta table schema, which requires the source-side and format settings that the following sections describe. Zerobus is partitionless, and it ingests only the record value. It does not persist record keys, headers, partition assignments, or timestamps.

The Kafka-compatible endpoint must be enabled for the workspace. If it is not enabled, authentication fails with Access denied: feature "Zerobus Ingest Kafka Endpoint" is not enabled for workspace "<workspace-id>". Error Code: 4062.

To use this route, set hypercdc.sink.type to kafka and configure the following producer properties:

Property Description

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.bootstrap.servers

The Zerobus Kafka endpoint, for example <workspace-id>.zerobus.<region>.cloud.databricks.com:9092.

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.security.protocol

Must be set to SASL_SSL.

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.sasl.mechanism

Must be set to OAUTHBEARER.

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.sasl.login.callback.handler.class

Must be set to io.hypercdc.server.databricks.zerobus.ZerobusOAuthBearerLoginCallbackHandler.

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.sasl.jaas.config

The JAAS configuration for the OAuthBearerLoginModule, which supplies the OAuth options that the login callback handler reads.

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.acks

Must be set to all.

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.enable.idempotence

Must be set to false. Zerobus does not implement the transactional APIs, so it rejects the InitProducerId request that the Kafka producer sends when idempotence is enabled. The producer then fails with UnsupportedVersionException: The node does not support INIT_PRODUCER_ID. Because Kafka clients enable idempotence by default, you must set this property explicitly.

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.compression.type

Must be set to none. Zerobus rejects compressed record batches.

Option Required Description

Yes

The OAuth client id (service principal application id).

Yes

The OAuth client secret for the service principal.

workspaceUrl

Yes, unless tokenEndpoint is set.

The Databricks workspace URL. The token endpoint is derived as <workspaceUrl>/oidc/v1/token.

Yes, unless audience is set.

The numeric workspace id. The token audience is derived as api://databricks/workspaces/<workspaceId>/zerobusDirectWriteApi.

Yes

A comma-separated list of fully qualified target tables (catalog.schema.table). The handler uses this list to build the OAuth Rich Authorization Requests (RFC 9396) authorization details, which grant the token the Unity Catalog privileges that Zerobus requires for the target tables.

tokenEndpoint

No

Overrides the OIDC token endpoint that is otherwise derived from workspaceUrl.

No

A bearer token, such as a personal access token, to use without modification. If you set this option, the handler skips the OAuth exchange and uses this token directly.
Record format for the Kafka route

Zerobus accepts a record value only if it is a JSON object whose fields match the target Delta table schema. A record that does not match is rejected with InvalidRecordException: This record has failed the validation on broker and hence will be rejected. To satisfy the requirement, configure the following options in addition to the producer properties:

Property Description

hypercdc.transforms

Apply the ExtractNewRecordState SMT so that the emitted record is a flat row rather than a change event envelope. Optionally apply the RegexRouter SMT to map the topic name to the fully qualified name of the target table.

hypercdc.format.value.schemas.enable

Must be set to false. Otherwise, the JSON converter wraps each value in a {"schema": …​, "payload": …​} envelope, which does not match the table schema.

hypercdc.source.decimal.handling.mode

Must be set to string. Zerobus rejects a JSON number for a DECIMAL column, and the default precise mode emits a Base64-encoded byte array. The string mode emits the exact decimal value as a JSON string, which Zerobus accepts.

hypercdc.source.time.precision.mode

Use the default adaptive mode, which emits a TIMESTAMP column as the number of microseconds since the epoch. Zerobus rejects an ISO-8601 string for a TIMESTAMP column, and it interprets a numeric value as microseconds. Because of the latter, the connect mode, which emits milliseconds, silently stores an incorrect instant.
Tuning throughput on the Kafka route

Throughput on the Kafka route is bound by network round trips rather than by local processing, because Zerobus acknowledges each request from the region in which the workspace runs. When the default producer settings are active, the number of records that the service ingests per second is approximately equal to the number of in-flight requests, multiplied by the number of records per request, and divided by the request latency. As a result, a pipeline that produces one record at a time spends most of its time waiting.

You can modify the default behavior by configuring the producer properties in the following table. Optimal values for these settings depend on the latency between the service and the workspace. Use the values in the table as starting points and adjust them based on latency data. To find the request latency of a running pipeline, read the request_latency_avg attribute of the standard kafka.producer:type=producer-metrics MBean, and to confirm that batching takes effect, read records_per_request_avg.

Property Suggested value Description

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.linger.ms

100

Specifies how long the producer waits to send requests. Requests accumulate until the configured interval passes.

Set the value to 0 to remove the delay interval so that the producer sends each request as soon as possible. When the property is set to 0, the producer sends requests even if they contain a small number of records. Because each request incurs the overhead of a full network round trip, when the producer has a high number of records to process, a 0 value can result in lower throughput.

Set a value greater than 0 if you want the producer to wait between sending requests. Setting a value greater than 0 can improve throughput, because the producer batches more records per request.

In a change data capture pipeline, the end-to-end latency is typically much greater than the delay introduced by this setting, so the additional wait is usually negligible.

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.batch.size

1048576

Specifies the maximum size, in bytes, of a single batch. If linger.ms is set, set this option if you want the producer to send batches after their size reaches the configured limit. This setting overrides the linger.ms setting to allow the producer to send batches before the end of the configured wait time. Zerobus rejects records larger than 10 MB, so a batch size of 1 MB leaves ample headroom.

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.max.in.flight.requests.per.connection

10

Specifies the maximum number of unacknowledged requests that the producer can send before it receives a response. Increasing the value can improve throughput by allowing the producer to send additional requests before it receives acknowledgements from earlier requests. However, increasing the value can also result in records being delivered out of order if requests are retried.

Zerobus is partitionless and provides an at-least-once delivery guarantee, so strict record ordering is not guaranteed regardless of how you configure this property.

In standard Kafka environments where idempotence is enabled, max.in.flight.requests.per.connection must not exceed 5, because the idempotent producer only guarantees ordering and exactly-once semantics for up to five in-flight requests. The Kafka route for the Databricks Zerobus Ingest sink requires enable.idempotence=false, so you can set this property to a value greater than 5.

The following example shows a complete configuration for the Kafka route:

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.bootstrap.servers=<workspace-id>.zerobus.<region>.cloud.databricks.com:9092
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.security.protocol=SASL_SSL

    workspaceUrl="https://<workspace-host>" \
    workspaceId="<workspace-id>" \
    clientId="<client-id>" \
    clientSecret="<client-secret>" \
    tables="<catalog>.<schema>.<table>" ;
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.acks=all
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.enable.idempotence=false
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.compression.type=none
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.linger.ms=100
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.batch.size=1048576
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=10
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.key.serializer=org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.value.serializer=org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.interceptor.classes=io.hypercdc.server.databricks.zerobus.metrics.ZerobusProducerInterceptor

hypercdc.format.value=json
hypercdc.format.value.schemas.enable=false
hypercdc.source.decimal.handling.mode=string

hypercdc.transforms.unwrap.delete.tombstone.handling.mode=rewrite

Data type mapping

When the sink maps data types, rather than converting values based on their serialized JSON representation, it uses Kafka Connect logical type information to normalize values to a format that is compatible with the target Delta column. By basing conversions on logical types rather than on the JSON encoding of values, the sink can accommodate different source-side serialization settings and avoid invalid-type ingestion errors without requiring users to tune source-side *.handling.mode options.

DATE (epoch days)

Monitoring

You can use JMX metrics and connector log output to monitor the operational status and performance of the HyperCDC Databricks Zerobus Ingest sink.

The HyperCDC Databricks Zerobus Ingest sink supports the following delivery routes: zerobus (gRPC), zerobus-rest (REST), and the Kafka route. All three routes expose sink metrics over JMX under the object name hypercdc.zerobus:type=connector-metrics,context=sink,server=<route>,task=0, where <route> is grpc for the zerobus route, rest for the zerobus-rest route, or kafka for the Kafka route. The metrics use the same JMX exposure model as the JDBC sink connector and HyperCDC source connectors, so existing JMX monitoring tools such as JConsole, jmxterm, and Prometheus JMX Exporter can read them without any Zerobus-specific configuration.

The sink registers the metrics when it starts, so no option is required to begin collecting them. Reading them from outside the process is a separate step: the service exposes JMX only after you set the JMX_HOST and JMX_PORT environment variables, and it starts the bundled Prometheus JMX Exporter only after you set JMX_EXPORTER_PORT. The HyperCDC monitoring documentation provides details about how to expose metrics by using JMX. You can automate periodic metric logging by setting hypercdc.sink.zerobus.metrics.log.interval or hypercdc.sink.zerobus-rest.metrics.log.interval to a positive value. After you enable either of these options, at the specified interval the connector writes an INFO log message that contains the same metric values that are available through JMX.

The Kafka route is the exception to metrics being collected automatically: because it writes through the generic kafka sink, the Zerobus sink is never invoked and cannot instrument itself. On that route the metrics are not collected until you register the following producer interceptor, which reports the same attributes under server=kafka:

hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.interceptor.classes=io.hypercdc.server.databricks.zerobus.metrics.ZerobusProducerInterceptor

The interceptor reads the operation and the source timestamp from the record headers, and falls back to scanning the serialized value when the headers are absent. Because the interceptor runs for every produced record, prefer the headers on a high-volume pipeline: configure the ExtractNewRecordState SMT with add.headers=op,source.ts_ms in addition to add.fields, as shown in Kafka route. Zerobus does not persist record headers, so the metadata does not reach the target table, and reading it from a header rather than scanning the value makes the interceptor several times cheaper per record. To enable periodic metric logging on this route, set hypercdc.sink.kafka.producer.zerobus.metrics.log.interval to a positive value. The option is the counterpart of hypercdc.sink.zerobus[rest].metrics.log.interval, except that it counts records rather than batches, because a producer interceptor observes individual sends. Two attributes carry a route-specific meaning: TotalFlushes counts broker-acknowledged records, which is the durability boundary on this route, and TotalRecordsSkipped remains 0, because the generic sink forwards every record that it receives.

On the Kafka route the interceptor times one in every 128 records rather than every record, so that LastFlushDurationMillis and MaxFlushDurationMillis describe a representative sample. Reading the system clock is significantly more expensive when the producer’s network thread reads it concurrently, and on a high-volume pipeline that cost outweighs everything else the interceptor does. The first record is always timed, so the gauges report a value even on a pipeline that produces few records. All counters remain exact.

The standard kafka.producer:type=producer-metrics and kafka.producer:type=producer-topic-metrics MBeans remain available, and provide per-topic byte counts and request latencies that complement the sink metrics.

The following attributes are available:

Attribute Description

TotalRecordsIngested

Total number of change events that Zerobus durably accepted, across all tables. On the gRPC route the sink counts a record only after the flush that covers it succeeds, so a batch that fails to flush never advances this metric.

TotalInserts / TotalUpdates / TotalDeletes / TotalReads

These metrics report the number of ingested events sorted by operation type (c / u / d, and snapshot reads r).

TotalRecordsSkipped

Number of records skipped without being forwarded (tombstones / null payloads, and events whose destination is not a fully qualified catalog.schema.table, such as schema-history or DDL events). The value remains 0 on the Kafka route, which forwards every record that it receives.

TotalErrors

Number of ingestion or flush failures observed.

TotalFlushes

The metric counts one of the following operations, depending on the route configuration:

  • Stream flush operations (gRPC route).

  • Successful record POST requests (REST route).

  • Broker-acknowledged records (Kafka route).

For the REST and Kafka routes, a successful POST or acknowledgement indicates that the record has been durably accepted and is no longer at risk of loss due to a service failure.

MilliSecondsBehindSource

Indicates the age, in milliseconds, of the most recently processed event. The value is calculated as current time - source.ts_ms. The metric reports the value -1 until after the Delta table ingests an event that contains a source timestamp. Values near 0 indicates that the sink is catching up to, or is synchronized with, the source.

This metric is a primary indicator of pipeline freshness in a CDC-to-lakehouse deployment.

MilliSecondsSinceLastEvent

Indicates the time that elapsed since the sink last forwarded an event. The metric reports the value -1 until the sink forwards the first event.

Use this metric together with MilliSecondsBehindSource. Because MilliSecondsBehindSource reports the age of the last event that the sink processed, its value stops changing if the pipeline stops, and, as a result, an idle source cannot be distinguished from a stalled sink. By contrast, if the value of MilliSecondsSinceLastEvent grows while the source database is known to be receiving writes, the pipeline is stalled.

LastFlushDurationMillis

Duration of the most recent flush (gRPC), record POST (REST), or broker acknowledgement (Kafka) operation. On the Kafka route the value describes a sampled subset of records rather than every record, as the following note describes.

MaxFlushDurationMillis

Longest duration of any flush (gRPC), record POST (REST), or broker acknowledgement (Kafka) operation since the task started. On the Kafka route the value describes a sampled subset of records rather than every record, as the following note describes.

ActiveStreams

Number of currently open Zerobus streams (one per target table). For the REST and Kafka routes, which do not open persistent streams, this value is always 0.

Connected

Indicates whether the sink currently holds a usable connection to Zerobus. On the gRPC route the value reflects the state of the SDK client, and on the REST route the state of the HTTP client. On the Kafka route the value is always true while metrics are reported, because a producer interceptor observes records rather than connection state. To monitor the connection on the Kafka route, use the standard kafka.producer:type=producer-metrics attributes.

Route

The delivery route these metrics belong to (grpc, rest, or kafka).

Extensions

HyperCDC Server uses the Quarkus framework and relies on dependency injection to enable developer to extend its behaviour. Note that only the JVM mode of Quarkus is supported, but not native execution via GraalVM. The server can be extended in two ways by providing a custom logic:

  • implementation of a new sink

  • customization of an existing sink - i.e. non-standard configuration

Implementation of a new sink

The new sink can be implemented as a CDI bean implementing interface HyperCDCEngine.ChangeConsumer and with annotation @Named and unique name and scope @Dependent. The name of the bean is used as the hypercdc.sink.type option.

The sink needs to read the configuration using Microprofile Config API. The execution path must pass the messages into the target system and regularly commit the passed/processed messages.

See the Kinesis sink implementation for further details.

Customization of an existing sink

Some of the sinks exposes dependency injections points that enable users to provide its own bean that would modify the behaviour of the sink. Typical examples are fine tuning of the target client setup, the destination naming etc.

See an example of a custom topic naming policy implementation for further details.

Transformation for Operation Code

By default, Cassandra connector has it’s own Operation Codes which are not entirely compatible with HyperCDC Operation Codes. If needed, a specific transform can be defined in HyperCDC Server’s application.properties to enable the conversion:

hypercdc.transforms=EnvelopeTransformation
hypercdc.transforms.EnvelopeTransformation.type=io.hypercdc.connector.cassandra.transforms.EnvelopeTransformation

This will convert Operation Codes as follows:

INSERT "i"          -> CREATE "c"
UPDATE "u"          -> UPDATE "u"
DELETE "d"          -> DELETE "d"
RANGE_TOMBSTONE "r" -> TRUNCATE "t"

Also please reach out if you have requirements for specific sinks to be supported by Debezium Server or even would be interested in contributing the required implementation. Debezium provides a ready-to-use application that streams change events from a source database to messaging infrastructure like Amazon Kinesis, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Apache Pulsar, Redis (Stream), or NATS JetStream. For streaming change events to Apache Kafka, it is recommended to deploy the Debezium connectors via Kafka Connect. Installation To install the server download and unpack the server distribution archive: Debezium Server distribution The above links refers to the nightly snapshot build of the Debezium main branch. If you are looking for a non-snapshot version, please select the appropriate version of this documentation in the menu to the right. A directory named debezium-server will be created with these contents: debezium-server/ |-- CHANGELOG.md |-- config |-- CONTRIBUTING.md |-- COPYRIGHT.txt |-- debezium-server-3.7.0.Beta1-runner.jar |-- lib |-- LICENSE-3rd-PARTIES.txt |-- LICENSE.txt |-- README.md `-- run.sh The server is started using run.sh script, dependencies are stored in the lib directory, and the directory config contains configuration files. In case of using the Oracle connector you will have to add to the lib directory the ORACLE JDBC driver (if using XStream also the XStream API files), explained here: Obtaining the Oracle JDBC driver and XStream API files Configuration Debezium Server uses MicroProfile Configuration for configuration. This means that the application can be configured from disparate sources like configuration files, environment variables, system properties etc. Configuration properties that contain the $ character are normally interpreted by Quarkus for property expansion. If a property value includes a $ character as a prefix, such as ${my.property}, the Microprofile configuration parser determines that the value is a property expression and attempts to expand it. To prevent the parser from attempting to expand values that use this syntax, escape the $ prefix with a second $ character; that is, provide the value as $${my.property}. The value of the property is then passed to Debezium as ${my.property}. The main configuration file is config/application.properties. There are multiple sections configured: debezium.source is for source connector configuration; each instance of Debezium Server runs exactly one connector debezium.sink is for the sink system configuration debezium.format is for the output serialization format configuration debezium.transforms is for the configuration of message transformations debezium.predicates is for the configuration of message transformation predicates An example configuration file can look like so: debezium.sink.type=kinesis debezium.sink.kinesis.region=eu-central-1 debezium.source.connector.class=io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector debezium.source.offset.storage.file.filename=data/offsets.dat debezium.source.offset.flush.interval.ms=0 debezium.source.database.hostname=localhost debezium.source.database.port=5432 debezium.source.database.user=postgres debezium.source.database.password=postgres debezium.source.database.dbname=postgres debezium.source.topic.prefix=tutorial debezium.source.schema.include.list=inventory In this configuration file example: The sink is setup for AWS Kinesis in region eu-central-1 The source connector is setup for PostgreSQL using the default Debezium decoderbufs plugin. If using PostgreSQL’s built-in pgoutput plugin, set debezium.source.plugin.name=pgoutput The source connector is set to capture events from a schema named inventory. If you want to capture all changes in the database, remove this line. Otherwise, update this line to correspond to your preferred schema or tables. The source offset will be stored in a file named offsets.dat in the data directory. Note that you might need to create this directory to prevent an error on startup.
